name: Senegal
summary_text: Senegal criminalises same-sex sexual activity under Article 319 of the 1965 Penal Code, which carries a maximum of five years' imprisonment. The provision is enforced: in September 2018 four LGBT people, two women and two men, were detained in Dakar on charges of "acts against the order of nature" after videos of them circulated, part of a wave of politically motivated detentions in the run-up to the 2019 elections.  A campaign to raise the maximum penalty to 15 years has run since 2020, with anti-LGBT forces pressing for the increase as of July 2024. The maximum sentence remains five years; the proposal has not been reported as enacted.  Official hostility extends to speech on the subject. A political activist and a preacher were jailed and fined 100,000 CFA francs each after posting a video attacking opposition leader Ousmane Sonko for allowing a visiting French politician to express support for same-sex marriage. The US State Department's 2012 human rights report on Senegal listed pre-electoral violence, torture, and violence and discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender persons among the country's major human-rights problems.  Violence by non-state actors is documented at extreme scale. In November 2023 the body of a 31-year-old man, named locally as Cheikh Fall, was dug up from a cemetery and burned in the street after it became known that he was gay. Four men were arrested in connection with the incident; images from the scene show a crowd of hundreds gathered around the fire.

name: Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha
summary_text: The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 code of practice on single-sex services do not automatically extend to Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha. Local law governs the territory, and those United Kingdom measures can apply only by Order in Council.  Consensual same-sex activity has been lawful in the territory since 2001, and the age of consent is equalised at 16 across Saint Helena, Ascension Island and Tristan da Cunha.  The 2009 constitutional order imposed by the United Kingdom bans discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation territory-wide, and those protections have been in force since 2009.  Same-sex marriage was legislated island by island. The Ascension Island Council approved the marriage ordinance on 31 May 2016 by 5 votes to 0; it was signed and gazetted on 20 June 2016 and commenced on 1 January 2017. Tristan da Cunha followed on 4 August 2017 and Saint Helena on 20 December 2017.  Adoption by same-sex couples has been permitted since 2017.  The territory is classified as an Overseas Country or Territory of the European Union, with applicability of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights recorded on that basis.
